content:
I experimented with LLM-based “fuzzing”. What to do with the insane amount of bugs found? Open them one by one on GitHub, or dump them into a tar archive and upload it as attachment in one single ticket?
The bugs are validated, but the explanations may be low quality. Or just publish the proven snippets without the explanations?
I'm curious ... how did you do it?
Are they all the same bug repeated, or really different bugs?

I'm curious ... how did you do it?

Nothing special, just trying different prompts and analysing the tool traces to see how the agents approach the problems, and how could be better guided towards exploring obscure corner cases.

The way I have been doing things is one at a time, having an Agent "find the root cause" using a worktree of Roc so I can be sure it's a higher quality bug report. Would you have capacity to work through them like that one at a time?

I guess one at a time would be more helpful

Are they all the same bug repeated, or really different bugs?

Yes, different bugs. I manually validated some of the examples.
I appreciate lots of bug reports as long as they're real! :smile:

The way I have been doing things is one at a time, having an Agent "find the root cause" using a worktree of Roc so I can be sure it's a higher quality bug report.

Unfortunately, I'm not familiar with the compiler source, so I can't check whether the agent actually found the root cause.

I appreciate lots of bug reports as long as they're real! :smile:

Should I open them one by one? Or put in one ticket?
github issues are fine, and honestly no need to find a root cause - steps to reproduce in a minimal example of the most helpful
up to you as to how to group them!
I'll open a bunch of them manually. I'll post the reproducer snippet and the outputs. If I should change something in the format or the method, let me know.
I opened a few tickets. If these are useful, I'll open more.
They look good :thumbs_up:

One thought @notramo is using a ReleaseSafe or Debug build instead of a nightly... then the reports wont be segfault but you can likely provide a more targeted failure. It's not necessary or anything, but seeing that detail helps to categorize the bug.
Knowing the nightly segfaults is helpful though too

Also if you mention the source of the bug, like "This was found using AI assisted fuzzing" or something then it helps to understand if this is blocking someone's current work which would attract a more urgent priority. I'm sure all the bugs will get fixed quickly, but as we find more it may get to a point we just have to pick the most urgent and priority ones off first

One thought notramo is using a ReleaseSafe or Debug build instead of a nightly... then the reports wont be segfault but you can likely provide a more targeted failure. It's not necessary or anything, but seeing that detail helps to categorize the bug.

Unfortunately, my machine don't have enough resources to compile a ReleaseSafe or Debug build. But I think it's not that necessary, because copy-pasting the snippet is ~3 seconds, and maintainers can check it with their own debug builds.

Also if you mention the source of the bug, like "This was found using AI assisted fuzzing" or something then it helps to understand if this is blocking someone's current work which would attract a more urgent priority.

I'll add it from now on.

Also if you mention the source of the bug, like "This was found using AI assisted fuzzing" or something then it helps to understand if this is blocking someone's current work which would attract a more urgent priority.

Is this really needed for every issue? I think it's better to write "This is blocking me." than "This is not blocking me."

First, I often find bugs manually while coding, but can easily work around and leave a TODO to remove the workaround hack when fixed upstream. These would not get the LLM label, but are not blocking me.

Second, I find many high-quality reports using LLMs, but also low quality corner cases too. Some of the high quality ones are causing silent logic errors or data loss, that are not obvious, and may be affecting somebody in production, despite not noticing it.
These get the LLM label despite being important.
I dont see the LLM thing as a negative

Is it enough to write this at the very low priority, corner cases like "parser crashes with this weird syntax that nobody would write during normal coding", or also apply to the very high quality ones?

I dont see the LLM thing as a negative

Me neither. It's just noise, because don't necessarily reflects the quality or urgency of the issue.

It's just helpful I think to know how the bug was discovered. It doesnt diminish the bug at all.

If someone is working on a project or using Roc in production and there is a regression or something its helpful to know too.

It's just a LLM or fuzzer style bug typically is less likely to be something someone has run into and is currently blocking them.
Its also no necessary to include that or anything. You just asked for ideas that might help
I try to guide the LLMs towards realistic bugs that can appear during actual programming scenarios. It turns out they are quite good at finding realistic bugs when it's explicitly stated as a goal.
yeah "this is blocking me" is the useful signal :smile:
for prioritization
Should I report when roc check hangs too? E.g. some infinite recursion. Should the comptime evaluation have a timeout (fuel limit)? Or is this expected?
short answer is that we don't need a report for it
@notramo See https://github.com/roc-lang/roc/issues/11334 for a little more context. (That's an issue I filed for essentially the same thing you're saying, unless I misunderstand you.)
I thought there was some kind of limit which failed to trigger, but if it's the intended behavior, it's okay for me.
What about hangs where it's not caused by comptime eval? For example, the type checker is stuck in a loop?
@Richard Feldman, should I report those, or not?
yeah! That should never happen
